The doctrinal evolution of the First Amendment from New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) through Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) can be traced through several key cases that refined the legal standards for freedom of speech and press. 

New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) (ID: 376_0254-01) established that public officials must prove "actual malice" to win a libel case against critics of their official conduct. This set a high bar for such cases, protecting freedom of the press to report on and criticize government officials.

Following this, in Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts (1967) (ID: 388_0130-01), the Court further defined the "actual malice" standard, holding that it applied not just to public officials but also to public figures, though the standard for the latter could be slightly different depending on the circumstances of the case.

The case of Street v. New York (1969) (ID: 394_0576-01) dealt with the issue of flag burning as a form of protest and the First Amendment protections afforded to such symbolic speech. The Court held that the government could not punish an individual for speaking defiant or contemptuous words about the American flag, further expanding the scope of protected speech.

Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) (ID: 395_0444-01) marked a significant point in this evolution, as it established the "imminent lawless action" test for speech that incites violence. The Court ruled that the government could only prohibit speech that is "directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action" and is "likely to incite or produce such action." This test narrowed the circumstances under which speech could be restricted, providing stronger protections for freedom of speech.

Throughout these cases, the Court transitioned from establishing a high standard for libel cases involving public officials and figures to defining the limits of protected speech in the context of public protest and incitement to violence. The legal standard evolved to require a more direct and imminent connection between the speech and potential lawless action before the government could intervene, thereby strengthening First Amendment protections.

The intermediate precedents, including New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts, and Street v. New York, played crucial roles in shaping the Court's understanding of the First Amendment's scope and application, ultimately influencing the decision in Brandenburg v. Ohio. These cases collectively contributed to a more robust protection of free speech, underscoring the importance of a free and uninhibited press and the right to express opinions and engage in symbolic speech without undue fear of government reprisal.
